title: Family members are the main victims of these killings
title_zh: 这些凶杀案里，受害者大多是家里人

image.credit: Photo by mostafa meraji on Unsplash
image.author: mostafa meraji

lead: A new study looks at killings in Spain. The person who kills often has a mental disorder. The victims are usually family members.
lead_zh: 西班牙一项新研究调查了这类凶杀案。行凶者常常有精神疾病，受害者往往是家里人。
preview: Researchers in Spain studied more than 2,500 homicide cases. These cases went to court over ten years. About 10% of the killers had a mental
preview_zh: 西班牙的研究人员调查了2500多起凶杀案。这些案子在十年里上了法庭。大约10%的凶手有精神疾病。这些凶杀大多发生在家中。在26%的案子里，受害者是父母。
paragraphs: Researchers in Spain studied more than 2,500 homicide cases. These cases went to court over ten years. About 10% of the killers had a mental disorder. Most of these killings happened at home. In 26% of the cases, the victim was a parent.

The study says victims get little help. Only a few victims receive money or support. Family members are in the most danger. They live with the person and see them every day. Other family members also feel pain and fear.

The law often gives these killers very light sentences. Sometimes they go free. Then the victims get no money and no help. The researchers say this is a big problem. They want the health system to watch these families more closely.
The study is in the Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine. Josep Maria Tamarit and his team at the Open University of Catalonia wrote it. They say society must support these victims better.

研究说，受害者得到的帮助很少。只有少数受害者拿到钱或支持。家里人最危险。他们和病人住在一起，每天都能见到。其他家人也感到痛苦和害怕。
法律常常给这些凶手很轻的判决。有时他们不用坐牢。这样受害者就得不到钱，也得不到帮助。研究人员说，这是个大问题。他们希望医疗系统多关注这些家庭。
这项研究发表在《法医与法律医学杂志》上。约瑟普·马里亚·塔马里特和他在加泰罗尼亚开放大学的团队写了这篇文章。他们说，社会必须更好地帮助这些受害者。
body:
Researchers in Spain studied more than 2,500 homicide cases. These cases went to court over ten years. About 10% of the killers had a mental disorder. Most of these killings happened at home. In 26% of the cases, the victim was a parent.

The study says victims get little help. Only a few victims receive money or support. Family members are in the most danger. They live with the person and see them every day. Other family members also feel pain and fear.

The law often gives these killers very light sentences. Sometimes they go free. Then the victims get no money and no help. The researchers say this is a big problem. They want the health system to watch these families more closely.

The study is in the Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine. Josep Maria Tamarit and his team at the Open University of Catalonia wrote it. They say society must support these victims better.

title_original: Hidden violence: Family members as the main victims of homicides linked to mental disorders
summary_original: In recent decades, the social and legal perception of people with mental disorders who commit crimes has changed. Initially, people with mental disorders were considered dangerous. In recent decades, the social and legal perception of people with mental disorders who commit crimes has changed. Initially, people with mental disorders were considered dangerous. However, since the late 20th century, the paradigm has shifted at both social and legal levels, with people experiencing mental disorders often considered victims themselves, despite having committed intentional crimes.
In this new context, a team of researchers from the Universitat Oberta de Catalunya (UOC) has analyzed homicides committed in Spain to characterize those perpetrated by people with mental disorders and study the factors that determine who the victims are and the compensation awarded in legal proceedings. Their research is
published
in the
Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine
.
"The noble aim of avoiding stigmatizing people with mental disorders as dangerous can contribute to overlooking the serious situation of those who are victims of this violence or face a greater risk of victimization," explained Josep Maria Tamarit, a professor of criminal law at the UOC and coordinator of the Empirical and Applied Victimology research group (VICRIM). He coordinated this research together with professors Laura Arantegui and Alba Marsol, who are part of the same group. All three teach in the Faculty of Law and Political Science.
Analysis of 2,500 homicides in a decade
As part of the study, the researchers from the Digital Transformation and Governance Research Center (UOC-DIGIT) reviewed more than 2,500 homicide cases tried in Spanish courts. Of these cases, 10% involved perpetrators with some type of mental disorder. In the vast majority of cases, homicides committed by people with some type of mental disorder occurred in the home, with 26% being parricides (involving the killing of a parent).
According to the experts, the main objective of this open-access study was to shed light on a reality that has so far been overlooked: the lack of recognition and compensation for victims of lethal violence committed by people with mental disorders, an issue obscured by efforts to prevent the stigmatization of the perpetrators. In addition, the study found that only a small number of victims of such crimes received compensation or financial support, a disadvantage largely attributable to the intrafamilial nature of most incidents.
The issue is complex: When a person with a mental disorder intentionally assaults a family member, the consequences include both physical and psychological harm. Other family members are also affected.
Family ties as the greatest risk factor
However, in many cases, because of this tendency to avoid stigmatizing people with mental disorders, perpetrators are acquitted or receive minimal sentences. Meanwhile, victims, both direct and indirect, are left without any compensation.
"Family members are most at risk because they are the people who have the greatest contact with perpetrators. Society leaves this problem in the hands of families. It is also important to consider the tensions that can arise within family relationships, which are intensified by the stress caused by living with people with these types of disorders," explained Tamarit, who noted that these victims "do not receive sufficient support from institutions."
This legal and contextual situation can be "considered a systemic failure" because victims are not compensated. Moreover, in some cases, to obtain effective compensation, they must hire a lawyer and pursue criminal proceedings against a family member with a mental disorder.
"We don't have any data to report specific failures, but if one considers that more than 10% of homicides are committed by people who represent no more than 2% of the population, and whose mental health problems are known to the health care system in most cases, we should be able to improve the detection of cases involving risk and the monitoring of individuals and their families," said the UOC researcher.
Preventive and reparative measures
To prevent this type of homicide, particularly within the family setting, support for families provided by the public health care system should be strengthened, including follow-up care for cases where risk has been identified.
In the experts' view, it is essential to rethink the current approach to victimization and to focus on the specific characteristics of this form of victimization, which frequently occurs within the perpetrator's closest family circle.
"The health care system should increase the monitoring of cases, apply risk identification tools and improve the public support system for victims of violent crime. While several reforms have been introduced to improve support in cases of gender-based violence, other needs have so far remained overlooked," concluded Tamarit.
